title: WHY “MY CUP OVERFLOWS” IS MORE POWERFUL THAN MOST CHRISTIANS REALIZE
paragraphs: WHY “MY CUP OVERFLOWS” IS MORE POWERFUL THAN MOST CHRISTIANS REALIZE
You may have quoted Psalm 23 for years. But hidden inside one familiar sentence is a picture of God’s goodness that becomes breathtaking when you realize where David is sitting when he says it.
There is a sentence Christians whisper in hospital rooms.
They print it on mugs.
They underline it in Bibles.
They quote it when life is going well.
“My cup overflows.”
Beautiful words.
But perhaps we have made them so familiar that we have stopped feeling their weight.
Because David does not say these words while standing on a mountain celebrating a trouble-free life.
He says them at a table.
And according to the psalm, something disturbing is nearby.
Enemies.
“You prepare a table before me in the presence of my enemies.”
Then comes the oil.
“You anoint my head with oil.”
And then:
“My cup overflows.”
Psalm 23:5.
Read that sequence again slowly.
A table.
Enemies.
Oil.
An overflowing cup.
David is not describing a life from which every threat has disappeared.
He is describing what it is like to belong to a Shepherd whose goodness is greater than the danger surrounding His sheep.
That changes everything.
The Hebrew behind the famous phrase is wonderfully compact:
כּוֹסִי רְוָיָה
kōsî rəwāyāh
“My cup is abundance.”
Or, naturally expressed in English:
“My cup overflows.”
The Hebrew word כּוֹסִי (kōsî) means “my cup.” The final -î carries the sense of “my.”
Then comes רְוָיָה (rəwāyāh), a word communicating abundance or saturation—something richly filled.
David gives us an image of sufficiency that has crossed into abundance.
But we need to understand what he is—and is not—promising.
Psalm 23 is not a divine guarantee that every Christian will become wealthy.
It is not a secret formula for financial prosperity.
It does not mean faithful believers will never experience cancer, grief, persecution, unemployment, betrayal, depression, loneliness, or death.
David himself knew suffering.
He knew what it was to be hunted.
He knew betrayal.
He knew warfare.
He knew family devastation.
He knew the consequences of his own terrible sin.
Yet this same man could look toward God and say:
“My cup overflows.”
Maybe that is why the sentence carries so much power.
Overflow does not necessarily mean you have everything you wanted.
Sometimes overflow means you discovered that God Himself was enough when almost everything else disappeared.
And somebody reading this knows exactly what that feels like.
You have smiled for photographs while quietly falling apart.
You have answered, “I’m okay,” because explaining the truth would have taken too long.
You have encouraged everyone else while wondering who would encourage you.
You have worshiped while carrying questions you were afraid to say aloud.
Maybe you prayed for something that never happened.
Maybe somebody left.
Maybe somebody died.
Maybe you failed.
Maybe the person who wounded you claimed to love God.
Maybe the deepest scandal in your story is not what somebody did to you.
Maybe it is what you did.
And perhaps that is the part nobody knows.
The browser history.
The secret messages.
The bitterness.
The affair.
The addiction.
The compromise.
The resentment.
The pride.
The money.
The lie.
The hidden habit.
The version of yourself that appears at church and the version that exists when nobody is watching.
You know the vocabulary of Christianity.
But lately your soul has felt empty.
And here comes David saying something almost offensive to exhausted people:
“My cup overflows.”
How?
Look again at the verse.
“You prepare a table before me in the presence of my enemies.”
God does not wait until every enemy leaves before preparing the table.
That matters.
We often tell God:
“Remove this, and then I will have peace.”
“Fix them, and then I will worship.”
“Answer this prayer, and then I will trust You.”
“Change my circumstances, and then I will know You are good.”
But Psalm 23 gives us another picture.
The enemies remain present.
And God prepares the table anyway.
The threat is real.
But so is the Host.
The valley was real earlier in the psalm too:
“Even though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death…”
David never pretends darkness is imaginary.
Biblical faith is not denial.
Christianity does not ask you to look at a grave and pretend it does not hurt.
It does not ask a betrayed spouse to call betrayal good.
It does not ask the persecuted believer to pretend persecution is pleasant.
It does not ask the grieving mother to stop crying.
Jesus Himself wept.
The Gospel does something infinitely greater than teaching us to pretend darkness is light.
It announces that darkness does not get the final word.
That is why Psalm 23 ultimately becomes even more beautiful when read in the light of Jesus Christ.
David begins:
“The LORD is my shepherd.”
Centuries later Jesus says:
“I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep.”
John 10:11.
Do not miss what Christianity is claiming.
The Shepherd does not merely point frightened sheep toward safety.
The Shepherd gives Himself for them.
And this is where the overflowing cup becomes painfully beautiful.
Because before resurrection morning…
before the empty tomb…
before victory was announced…
Jesus entered suffering.
In Gethsemane He prayed concerning the “cup” before Him.
“My Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me; nevertheless, not as I will, but as you will.”
Matthew 26:39.

The Bible uses the imagery of a cup in different ways depending on context, including blessing and judgment. We should not carelessly collapse every biblical reference to a cup into one identical symbol.
But the contrast should still humble us.
David speaks of a cup characterized by abundance.
Christ willingly goes toward the suffering appointed for Him.
At the cross, Jesus bears sin and gives His life for sinners.
Not because humanity deserved rescue.
Because grace is grace precisely because we did not.
That is the scandal at the center of Christianity.
The innocent One condemned.
The guilty offered forgiveness.
The Holy One surrounded by sinners.
The King wearing thorns.
The Shepherd dying for sheep who wandered away.
Jesus Christ crucified.
And then—
the grave loses.
Christ rises.
Suddenly “my cup overflows” becomes more than a decorative sentence for comfortable days.
For the Christian, our deepest abundance is not measured by what is parked in the driveway.
It is measured by what happened at an empty tomb.
Forgiven.
Reconciled.
Adopted.
Redeemed.
Given hope beyond death.
Invited to the table of a King we once rebelled against.
That is overflow.
You can lose money and still possess Christ.
You can lose popularity and still possess Christ.
You can lose the approval of people and still possess Christ.
You can walk through grief while being held by Christ.
You can stand beside a grave and still possess a hope death cannot ultimately destroy.
This does not make suffering small.
It makes Jesus greater.
And perhaps somebody needs that distinction today.
God's goodness is not proven by the absence of valleys.
Psalm 23 itself destroys that idea.
The Shepherd is good even while the sheep walk through the valley.
The Shepherd is present even while enemies watch.
The Shepherd provides even before circumstances become comfortable.
And David does not merely say the cup is full.
It overflows.
There is something deeply convicting about overflow because overflow was never meant merely to terminate on us.
Grace received begins reshaping the person who receives it.
The forgiven learn forgiveness.
The comforted begin comforting.
The rescued begin telling other prisoners where freedom can be found.
The person who has tasted mercy begins saying:
“You need to meet the One who met me.”
Maybe this is why your scars survived.
Not because God enjoyed your pain.
But because healed scars can sometimes become signposts pointing wounded people toward the Healer.
Peter failed spectacularly.
He denied Jesus.
Three times.
Imagine the shame when the rooster crowed.
Imagine remembering your own voice saying you did not know Him.
Peter's failure became public Scripture.
His worst night has been read for centuries.
Talk about scandal.
Yet Jesus did not throw Peter away.
After the resurrection, Christ restored him and commissioned him to care for His people.
Failure was not Peter's final chapter.
Grace rewrote what shame wanted to make permanent.
That does not mean sin did not matter.
It mattered enormously.
Grace is not God pretending rebellion is harmless.
Grace is why repentance becomes possible without despair.
We confess because sin is serious.
We run to Christ because His mercy is greater.
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
1 John 1:9.
Maybe you have spent years trying to hide the empty places in your cup.
Jesus already sees them.
Maybe you have spent years trying to fill them with attention.
Relationships.
Pornography.
Money.
Success.
Food.
Approval.
Ministry recognition.
Alcohol.
Achievement.
Endless scrolling.
Another purchase.
Another person.
Another promise to yourself that tomorrow you will finally become different.
Yet the soul remains thirsty.
Because some thirsts cannot be satisfied by putting more of the world into them.
Jesus said:
“If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink.”
John 7:37.
Come to Me.
Not perform for Me.
Not impress Me.
Not repair yourself sufficiently and then approach Me.
Come.
Repentance is not cleaning yourself enough to deserve Jesus.
Repentance is turning from sin toward the Savior because you finally understand that sin cannot give you what it promised.
The Gospel says Christ receives sinners who come to Him in faith.
Your scandal may explain part of your story.
It does not have to write the ending.
Jesus does that better.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
And perhaps right now your cup does not feel overflowing.
Perhaps it feels cracked.
Perhaps you feel like you have poured yourself into everyone until there is almost nothing left.
Then hear this carefully:
You do not have to manufacture overflow.
A cup cannot fill itself.
The Shepherd provides.
The Shepherd leads.
The Shepherd restores.
“He restores my soul.”
Psalm 23:3.
There may be someone reading these words with tears beginning to form because you have been trying to restore yourself.
You cannot.
But Christ can redeem what you surrender to Him.
Not necessarily by restoring every circumstance to the exact shape you wanted.
Sometimes His work is deeper than that.
He changes us.
He forgives.
He sanctifies.
He teaches us to trust.
He carries us through valleys.
He transforms wounds into compassion.
He exposes idols we thought we needed.
He teaches us that the greatest gift at God's table is ultimately God Himself.
And someday every believer in Christ will discover just how temporary the valley really was.
Psalm 23 ends:
“Surely goodness and mercy shall follow me all the days of my life, and I shall dwell in the house of the LORD forever.”
Forever.
That is the word suffering cannot defeat.
Forever.
Cancer does not get forever.
Grief does not get forever.
Temptation does not get forever.
The cemetery does not get forever.
Your enemies do not get forever.
Your shame does not get forever.
Jesus does.
And if you belong to Christ, your story is moving toward Him.
Maybe now you understand why “my cup overflows” is far more powerful than many Christians realize.
It is not the boast of someone who finally acquired enough possessions.
It is the testimony of someone who discovered the goodness of the Shepherd even with enemies nearby.
The table is prepared.
The Shepherd is present.
The cup is abundant.
And grace keeps spilling over the edges.
So do not keep this truth trapped on your screen.
If someone came to your mind while reading this, send it to them.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, be brave enough to comment, “Jesus, forgive me.”
If you are exhausted but still refusing to abandon your faith, comment, “I’m still fighting.”
If you need believers to stand with you in prayer, simply comment, “pray for me.”
Someone else may recognize their valley inside the story of how Christ carried you through yours.
It cannot.
Not because financial support earns salvation.
It never will.
Salvation is God's gift of grace, received through faith in Jesus Christ.
If you want another practical way to glorify God with the resources He has entrusted to you, supporting faithful Gospel ministry and sharing biblical truth can be part of that stewardship.
Not for applause.
Not to prove your spirituality.
Not because an algorithm can measure faithfulness.
One person hiding a scandal.
One marriage barely surviving.
One exhausted believer thinking about walking away.
One prodigal wondering whether Jesus would still receive them.
One person silently asking whether grace could possibly reach this far.
You may never know who reads because you shared.
But you can make sure they have the opportunity.
Share. Comment. Save the article. Pray for the ministry. Invite someone into Scripture.
Because the goal was never merely to build an audience.
The goal is to point people toward Jesus.
The Shepherd.
The Savior.
The crucified and risen King.
The One who meets sinners in their scandal and does not leave repentant sinners where He found them.
So tonight, when you whisper those familiar words again—
“My cup overflows”—
do not picture only money.
Do not picture only success.
Do not picture a painless life.
Picture a table surrounded by enemies.
Picture a Shepherd who has not abandoned His sheep.
Picture grace you could never purchase.
Picture forgiveness you could never earn.
Picture a cross where your Savior gave Himself.
Picture an empty tomb announcing that death does not have the last word.
Picture every undeserved mercy that carried you to this moment.
Then look at the cracks in your story.
Maybe they are not proof that the cup is useless.
Maybe they are places where people can finally see what has been filling it.
And remember this:
The world may remember the scandal that emptied you, but Jesus is still writing the grace that will overflow from you.
